docs.title: Sensez Docs
docs.text:
Sensez is the structural maintainability layer that sits beside your linter and type-checker. It looks for cross-file problems that are easy for an agent or a busy team to miss: duplication, dead code, import cycles, boundary violations, and design smells.

Start here:

  • Getting Started
  • CLI Reference
  • Finding Reference
  • Configuration Reference
  • Local Metrics
  • MCP and Agents
  • GitHub Action

docs.title: Getting Started
docs.text: Sensez is meant to run inside an agent loop so it can catch smells before they reach a pull request. The fastest path is to keep it close to the edit: use it inside your coding agent loop to provide it quick feedback on its work, as it's getting developed.

docs.title: 1. Install
docs.text:
PythonJS / TS 
# As a project dev dependency
uv add --dev sensez

# Or as a global CLI
uv tool install sensez

npm install --save-dev sensez

docs.title: 2. Initialize the repository
docs.text:
PythonJS / TS 
uv run sensez init

npx sensez init

sensez init setup guides you through the install, after you select which coding agent to use it with. Then:

  • writes a commented starter config — sensez.toml, or a [tool.sensez] section in pyproject.toml if you prefer;
  • registers the Sensez MCP server with your agent, so the agent launches Sensez automatically at startup;
  • installs the Sensez skill that teaches the agent when and how to scan;
  • creates .sensez/ for local metrics and caches, and adds it to .gitignore, if local metrics are enabled;
  • optionally installs an experimental end-of-turn gate hook (Claude Code only).

What init writes for each supported agent:

Agent MCP config Agent skill Gate hook Claude Code .mcp.json .claude/skills/sensez Optional, in .claude/settings.json Cursor .cursor/mcp.json — — Cline .cline/mcp.json .cline/skills/sensez — Codex .codex/config.toml .codex/skills/sensez — OpenCode opencode.jsonc .opencode/skills/sensez — Pi .pi/mcp.json .pi/skills/sensez — Other / none — (init prints guidance instead) — —

The MCP config starts node_modules/.bin/sensez when Sensez is a project dependency and the agent launches servers from the workspace root (Claude Code), or sensez when the running binary is the one on PATH. Otherwise it stores this machine's absolute path and init prints a note, since that entry will not work for teammates.

docs.title: 3. Restart your agent
docs.text: Agents load MCP servers at startup. Restart the agent (or reload the window) after init, or the sensez tools will not appear.

docs.title: 4. Tune it
docs.text: Everything Sensez does is configured in the file init wrote. Continue with the Configuration Reference for action levels, per-language overrides, boundary rules, and accepting findings, and the Finding Reference for what each detector does.

docs.title: Local metrics
docs.text:
Sensez records how it is used and how often its findings lead to real fixes, so it can prove its worth and tune itself over time. Everything is local-only. It lives under each repo's .sensez/local-metrics/ (gitignored). There is no OpenTelemetry, no network, no export of any kind. Disable per repo with:

[self_improvement]
enabled = false

Recording is automatic — the model is never asked to report (that would burn tokens). The only user-initiated input is triage_finding (a debt / false-positive verdict).

docs.title: Files on disk
docs.text:
File Contents Growth bound events.jsonl Append-only event log (one JSON object per line). The source of truth; everything else is derived. Compacted on flush once it passes 4 MB, keeping a 45-day window. totals.json Aggregates rebuilt by folding events. Most fields are all-time; reported_by_detector is the latest scan's current finding set. Bounded — keys are a finite pillar/<detector> space. last-scan.json Per-branch fingerprint baseline + resolved-history (for reintroduction detection). Capped at 32 branches (LRU); resolved-history entries expire after 30 days. triage.json The user's debt / false-positive verdicts, keyed by finding fingerprint. Grows only on explicit user verdicts.

A finding's fingerprint is its structural identity (symbols, modules, rules, participating files) — never line numbers or metric values — so moving code around never looks like a fix. Its detector is pillar/<kind> (e.g. smells/god_module, dead_code/function) or just the pillar for pillars without sub-kinds (cycles, boundaries, duplication).

docs.title: Events (events.jsonl)
docs.text:
• scan — a scan ran. Carries origin (tool | gate | cli), per-detector reported counts for that scan, per-detector resolved (findings that vanished since the last full scan, with summed time-to-resolution), reintroduced (previously resolved findings that came back, with summed interval), files/loc (size), and a config_hash.
  • search — a search_docs call: hit count, top score, bytes returned vs. referenced (context saved), and whether it was the first search on the repo.
  • auto_resolve — the server re-ran the pipeline after files changed and found previously-reported findings gone (no agent involvement).
  • gate_block — the end-of-turn gate blocked, with the fingerprints it flagged (input to block→fix conversion).
  • outcome — a user triage verdict (debt / false_positive), keyed by detector so per-detector precision is derivable.

docs.title: usage_report output
docs.text:
Backed by totals.json plus read-time derivations (brainz::report):

  • all_time.reported_by_detector — the latest persisted scan's current per-detector finding counts. Re-scanning unchanged code or switching away and back to the same branch must not inflate it as a lifetime counter.

  • precision_by_detector — (resolved + debt) / (resolved + debt + false_positive), with raw counts so a low-sample rate isn't mistaken for a confident one.

  • mean_resolution_days — per detector + _overall; how fast findings get fixed.
  • fix_reintroductions_by_detector — fixes that didn't stick: reintroduction count, reintroduction rate, and mean days a fix held.
  • gate_funnel — scans by origin and the gate's share (edit-time enforcement).
  • gate_conversion — of findings the gate blocked, how many were fixed vs. escaped open. conversion_rate is null until a full scan exists to measure against (the gate alone writes no baseline).
  • search_health — zero-hit rate over all searches.
  • self_health — mean_scan_ms, ms_per_kfile, ms_per_kloc: Sensez' own throughput, so a perf regression shows up in the same ledger as its findings.
  • config_pressure — how often the effective config changed, plus current scope (exclusion globs, boundary rules, threshold).
  • calibration — evidence-backed config-hygiene suggestions for the human to act on (Sensez never edits its own config).
  • recent_30d — the trust signals recomputed over the trailing 30 days, so trend is visible, not just the all-time average.
  • stale_findings / triaged — findings unresolved > 7 days (triage candidates) and the verdicts already recorded.

docs.title: How the metrics feed back
docs.text:
The collected data changes presentation, never the rules:

  • Ranking — findings from detectors below 0.5 precision (with ≥ 4 adjudications) sink to the back of scan and gate output, so trusted findings lead. The rule still fires; only order changes.
  • Gate escalation — a finding that was previously fixed (in the resolved-history, or blocked and then fixed within the gate's session) is flagged as a regression in the gate message.
  • Calibration — noisy detectors, hotspots, and never-fired boundary rules are surfaced as suggestions; the human edits sensez.toml.

docs.title: Refresh Flow
docs.text:
Each smell can provide example.py/fixed.py and example.ts/fixed.ts. For test smells, use test_example.py/fixed_test.py and example.test.ts/fixed.test.ts so the files remain real test sources. Add an exact-smells marker when the bad example must emit only its named smell; the verifier always requires the fixed example to emit no findings.

Regenerate generated reference pages after changing glossary metadata:

just docs-generate

To preview the rendered site:

just docs-serve

docs.title: Versioned Publishing
docs.text:
The public site is versioned with mike.

  • Pushes to main/master publish the moving dev docs version.
  • Full releases publish the Cargo/PyPI release version, for example 0.2.0.
  • The latest alias is updated to point at the newest full release.

To build a local versioned copy without pushing:

just docs-version 0.2.0
just docs-version-serve

Then review the diff and keep the prose pages short. If a page starts to repeat what the code already says, it should usually be rewritten to explain how to use the feature instead of describing it again.

docs.title: Style Rules
docs.text:
• Prefer task-oriented pages over long conceptual essays.
  • Put one idea on a page unless the topics are naturally inseparable.
  • Keep code snippets runnable and concrete.
  • Link to the source page for anything that is generated or mechanically derived.

docs.title: Exit codes
docs.text:
Code Meaning 0 Clean: the scan ran and no gate tripped 1 Gate tripped: a finding met --fail-on / --fail-on-new 2 Error: bad arguments, no usable diff for --diff / --diff-from / --fail-on-new, or an incomplete scan under --fail-on / --fail-on-new (an analyzer such as [duplication.semantic] could not run)

--diff and --diff-from never fall back to a full scan: outside a git work tree, or with an unreadable diff file, they exit 2. --fail-on without a diff flag works outside git.

docs.title: sensez --help
docs.text:
Sensez — the structural maintainability layer for your codebase.

Finds the cross-file problems linters and type-checkers can't see: duplication, dead code, import cycles, layering/boundary violations, and design smells. Opinionated guardrails that keep a codebase coherent and maintainable as it grows.

Run it alongside your linter and type-checker (e.g. Ruff/ty for Python, ESLint/tsc for JS/TS), not instead of them.

Usage: sensez [OPTIONS] [PATH] [COMMAND]

Commands:
  noze    Code smell and structure checks. Defaults to scanning the given path
  reflexez  Run only tests affected by current changes, using the existing test runner
  init    Set up a repository, or offer a global agent install outside Git
  mcp     MCP server commands
  brainz  Local metrics and value reports
  eyez    Docs/comment search commands
  help    Print this message or the help of the given subcommand(s)

Arguments:
  [PATH]
          Root directory of the target project when no subcommand is supplied

Options:
      --threshold <THRESHOLD>
          Minimum structural-token run length for the duplication detector (0 = off)

      --summary
          Emit aggregated per-rule JSON for configuration tuning

      --json
          Emit machine-readable JSON instead of a human-readable report

      --max <MAX>
          Cap each pillar to its top-N ranked findings; smells are capped per kind (0 = unlimited)

      --all
          Print every finding instead of the default top offenders

      --duplicates
          Report only duplicate-code findings

      --dead-code
          Report only high-confidence dead-code findings by default

      --cycles
          Report only circular-import findings

      --boundaries
          Report only boundary violations

      --smells
          Report only design-smell findings

      --output-glob <GLOB>
          Keep only output findings whose source file matches GLOB. Repeatable

      --diff
          Keep only findings touching the working-tree diff vs HEAD (uses git)

      --diff-from <FILE>
          Keep only findings touching a unified diff read from FILE ("-" = stdin)

      --fail-on [<LEVEL>]
          Exit non-zero if any finding meets or exceeds the given action level (must_fix | warning | advisory | info). Defaults to `must_fix` when the flag is present without a value

      --fail-on-new [<LEVEL>]
          Exit non-zero if diff-scoped findings meet or exceed the given action level (must_fix | warning | advisory | info). Defaults to `must_fix` when the flag is present without a value

      --explain
          Append a plain-English legend defining each finding category shown

  -h, --help
          Print help (see a summary with '-h')

  -V, --version
          Print version

docs.title: Output limits and gates
docs.text:
• By default each pillar shows its top 5 findings and smells show their top 3 per kind. --max N sets that cap for every pillar and every smell kind, so --smells --max 1 prints one finding per smell kind. --all prints every finding and cannot be combined with --max.
  • --fail-on and --fail-on-new see the findings this run selected: pillar flags such as --dead-code and --output-glob filter the gate too, and low-confidence dead code never trips it. The display cap does not: a finding hidden by --max still fails the gate.
  • Pillar flags leave the other pillars out of the report: the terminal omits their sections, and JSON lists them in meta.filtered_pillars, so a 0 total there means "not asked", not "clean".
  • --summary counts the same selected findings: it honours --diff, --diff-from, --fail-on-new, the pillar flags and --output-glob, and its exit code follows --fail-on / --fail-on-new like a normal run.
  • --output-glob '!PATTERN' excludes matching files (quote it for the shell). Includes and excludes combine: a finding is kept when its file matches an include (or no include is given) and no exclude. A clone group drops only its excluded occurrences and stays while two or more remain. ! alone or !!… is rejected (exit 2).
  • --fail-on-new implies --diff and says so on stderr. In diff mode the terminal report starts with "diff mode: only findings touching changed lines".
  • A level that is not must_fix, warning, advisory or info is rejected. --fail-on takes the next word as its level, so write sensez noze . --fail-on or --fail-on=must_fix ., not --fail-on ..

docs.title: Embedding model
docs.text:
eyez search, eyez reindex and [duplication.semantic] use the minishlab/potion-code-16M-v2 model at a pinned revision. It is looked up, in order:

  1. SENSEZ_EYEZ_MODEL_DIR: a directory holding config.json, tokenizer.json and model.safetensors. Nothing is downloaded.
  2. The HuggingFace cache: $HF_HOME/hub, else ~/.cache/huggingface/hub.
  3. A download (about 35 MB) into that cache. Sensez prints one line to stderr before it starts; HF_ENDPOINT changes the host.

With HF_HUB_OFFLINE=1 or SENSEZ_OFFLINE=1, step 3 is skipped and a missing model is an error that names the cache it checked.

docs.title: Configuration Reference
docs.text:
Sensez reads sensez.toml at the repository root. If that file is absent, it falls back to a [tool.sensez] table in pyproject.toml; when both exist, sensez.toml wins.

sensez init writes a starter file with every supported knob commented at its default — that generated file is the complete surface. This page explains the concepts behind it and the common tuning workflows. The sensez.toml Sensez uses on itself is a heavily commented real-world example.

docs.title: Validation
docs.text:
Sensez checks the whole file before it scans. Every problem is printed as sensez.toml:LINE:COL: message, with a "did you mean" hint where one fits.

  • Errors make Sensez ignore the whole file and scan with the default configuration: TOML syntax errors, wrong value types, invalid values such as cycles = "critical", and unknown keys inside [smells] (including [smells.rules.*] and the language tables) and [action].
  • Warnings ignore only the offending key and the scan continues: unknown keys in other tables ([duplication], [dead_code], [cycles], …) and unknown top-level tables.

Neither changes the exit code: a --fail-on / --fail-on-new run is still decided by its findings, and prints a gate: line on stderr noting that configuration issues were reported. Check the printed problems (or meta.issues, see below) in CI to catch a broken file.

MCP scan tools return the same problems as an error result. The end-of-turn gate and the language server keep working on defaults instead.

docs.title: Action levels
docs.text:
Every finding carries an action level. From quietest to strictest: info → advisory → warning → must_fix.

Action levels decide how automated workflows react:

  • sensez noze . --diff --fail-on-new [LEVEL] exits non-zero when diff-scoped findings meet or exceed LEVEL (default must_fix) — this is the CI hook.
  • Agents and the end-of-turn gate treat each pillar according to its level, so must_fix findings lead and info findings stay out of the way.

Pillar defaults: boundaries = must_fix, cycles = warning, duplication = advisory, dead_code = advisory. Smells inherit the severity of their detector. Override per pillar or per smell:

[action]
duplication = "warning"

[smells.rules.loose_typing]
action = "must_fix"

docs.title: Smell rules: base vs per-language
docs.text:
[smells.rules.<kind>] applies to every language. [smells.<lang>.rules.<kind>] — where <lang> is python, javascript, typescript, or rust — overrides the base for that language only. (The Rust profile is dogfooding-only and not shipped in the published packages.)

Setting any knob, including action, enables the rule; use enabled = false for explicit suppression. A rule's own action wins over the [action.smells] entry for the same smell. A flat threshold under [smells] or [smells.<lang>] (max_function_lines, max_cyclomatic, max_nesting, …) also enables its rule, unless the same table sets the rule's toggle (for example long_function = false) or lists it in disabled.

# All languages: long functions warn past 80 lines.
[smells.rules.long_function]
max_lines = 80
action = "warning"

# ...except TypeScript, which allows 120.
[smells.typescript.rules.long_function]
max_lines = 120

Every rule's knobs and default enabled state are listed in the Finding Reference.

docs.title: Dead code: teaching Sensez about your framework
docs.text:
Sensez ships no hardcoded framework names. Liveness is modeled from entry points, and your lists are merged with the language-profile defaults — you only add what is specific to your project:

[dead_code]
entrypoints = ["route", "fixture", "task"]   # decorator trailing names that register code
entrypoint_names = ["register", "main"]      # function/class names invoked dynamically
entrypoint_bases = ["AppConfig"]             # base classes loaded dynamically
entry_points = ["**/scripts/**"]             # file globs reached outside the import graph
test_sources = ["**/*.e2e.ts"]               # extra test-runner globs (test roots)
test_support = ["**/testing/**"]             # extra test-helper globs
orphan_modules = true                        # report modules no root reaches
unimported_dir_share = 50                    # % of a directory's modules nothing imports that marks it runtime-loaded (0 = off)

Dead code walks the import graph from two kinds of roots:

  • Production roots: entry_points globs, manifest entries (pyproject.toml scripts, Cargo binaries and lib.rs, package.json main / module / bin / exports, where a dist/, lib/, build/ or out/ target also names its src/ twin, and source files a package.json scripts command or a .github/workflows run: step runs, and JS/TS files with a shebang or a top-level main guard such as import.meta.main or require.main === module), and tool configs such as *.config.ts. An entry-point file is never reported, and its imports count as usage.
  • Runtime-loaded directories: when at least unimported_dir_share percent (default 50) of the modules under a directory, and at least five of them, have no runtime importer (tests and type-only imports do not count), Sensez takes the runtime to load that directory by path, as frameworks, plugin folders and serverless function folders do. Those modules become production roots and are not reported. Set unimported_dir_share = 0 to turn this off.
  • Test roots: test_sources globs plus the profile's test files.

A symbol that only tests import is reported at Medium with reason = "test_only". Files matching test_support (JS/TS default: **/e2e/**, **/test-utils/**, **/testUtils/**, **/fixtures/**, **/__fixtures__/**) are test helpers: their test importers count as users, so only truly unused helpers are reported.

Reachability is a property of whole modules, so it is reported once per module with kind module, at Medium, anchored at the first unused symbol, with symbol listing the unused names. A module that nothing imports and no root reaches has reason = "unreachable_module"; add its path to entry_points if a tool runs it, or set orphan_modules = false. A module only tests reach has reason = "test_only".

Names a barrel re-exports (export { x } from "./x") count as used in their defining module only when someone imports them from the barrel (chains and export * included). An unused name is reported once, where it is defined; the barrel line itself is never reported.

A whole-namespace type import (import type * as jobs, as generated API manifests use) keeps its exports at Medium. When the same initializer callee (export const run = task({ ... }), builder chains included) initializes at least five exports across the modules such a manifest exposes, Sensez treats that callee as a registration and those exports as live.

Confidence is High unless evidence suggests hidden use, then Medium: a default export, an importer that binds the module whole or not at all (import(), import mod), a type-only namespace reference, an import from a tool config, test-only use, or an unreachable module.

entrypoints and entrypoint_names accept a trailing * as a prefix pattern (entrypoint_names = ["on*"]). entrypoint_names also applies to methods under unused_methods. For JS/TS methods only, React lifecycle, custom-element and test-reporter callback names are live by default, and methods of a class that extends or implements anything outside the scan are not reported (they may be framework hooks). In JS/TS, entrypoints matches the callee of an exported initializer, so entrypoints = ["register", "define*"] keeps export const send = register({ ... }) alive.

If dead-code output feels incomplete, broader unused-symbol classes are available as opt-ins (your generated config shows their defaults):

[dead_code]
unused_imports = true
unused_methods = true

Unused module-level variables and constants are off by default; set unused_variables = true to report them.

Prefer adding entry points over suppressing individual findings — one line of config fixes a whole class of false positives.

docs.title: Duplication
docs.text:
[duplication]
threshold = 50   # minimum structural-token run to report a clone; raise to quieten, 0 disables
max_gap = 25     # stitch clones across small consistent edits; 0 disables
exclude = ["**/tests/**", "**/migrations/**"]   # clone-only excludes (files stay in the graph)
include_tests = false       # true also compares test files
include_generated = false   # true also compares generated files

Duplication and smells skip, on top of exclude:

  • Test files matched by the language profile (JS/TS: __tests__/, *.test.*, *.spec.*, tests/, test/, plus __mocks__/, __fixtures__/, e2e/, test-utils/ and *.stories.*) and the built-in tests/, test/ and pytest file names. The Python profile also counts examples/ and docs_src/, and the Rust profile benches/, so those are skipped too. Set include_tests = true under [duplication] or [smells] to analyse them. weak_test_oracle and fixture_echo_assertion always inspect test files.
  • Generated files (JS/TS): paths under _generated/ or __generated__/, *.gen.* and *.generated.*, or a first-1 KB header containing @generated, do not edit, auto-generated, automatically generated or code generated by. They stay in the graph for cycles and dead code, but never count as smell hotspots or importers for god_module and shotgun_surgery_hazard.
  • Migrations: migrations/, plus alembic/ and versions/ for Python files only.

sensez noze . --summary lists the effective excludes and skip counts under scope, and the human report prints one dimmed line under Duplication when files were skipped.

Structural matching keeps member, property and type names, so a copy that renames only locals is still a clone. Whole functions at least twice the threshold are also compared after a consistent rename of every name and literal, so a copy that renames its members is found too. near_miss = true extends that rename pass to functions down to threshold.

Opt-in detectors for harder clones: class_name_duplicates, class_property_overlap_min, and [duplication.semantic] (only in builds with the eyez feature). If the semantic pass is enabled but its embedding model cannot load (for example offline with no cached model), the scan prints an analyze issue on stderr, and --fail-on / --fail-on-new exit 2 with "incomplete scan" rather than passing. JSON output lists the issue under meta.issues only when SENSEZ_SCAN_DIAGNOSTICS or SENSEZ_TIMING is set.

[duplication.semantic]
enabled = true
min_shape_score = 30       # token 4-gram overlap (0-100) separating edited copies from rewrites; above 100 is an error
comment_boost_score = 85   # doc similarity (50-100) that confirms an edited copy; below 50 is an error
comment_required = false   # true compares documented functions only

Semantic groups only consider functions of at least threshold tokens. Each pair is scored four ways: structural overlap (4-gram Jaccard), and the cosine, under the code embedding model, of the two functions' source, of their signatures (name and parameter words, ignoring words that many functions in the codebase share) and of their doc comments. A group carries one of two verdicts:

  • semantic: edited copy (structure 0.48, code 0.91, names 0.88, docs n/a): overlap at least min_shape_score, confirmed by similar source and similar signatures, or by matching doc comments. Reported at the duplication action level.
  • semantic: same intent, structurally different code (structure 0.12, code 0.86, names 0.92, docs n/a): a rewrite of the same function, for example a loop and a filter/map chain. Reported as info.

Pairs are only compared when they share enough uncommon structure, signature words or doc words; words and shapes used by most functions in the codebase never pair two functions on their own.

When several detectors report the same code, the widest group is kept, its line ranges grow to cover the others, and the folded groups are listed under absorbed in JSON output. Each group's source is in detector. The hint says the token count (a range when a folded group is wider), the number of copies, what to do, and how many overlapping groups were folded in.

docs.title: Cycles
docs.text:
[cycles]
exclude = ["**/vendor/**"]   # import edges here never report a cycle
include_type_only = true     # also report cycles closed only by type imports

A cycle that only exists through type-level imports (TypeScript import type, Python if TYPE_CHECKING:) is reported at info with a "type coupling" hint. Set include_type_only = false to drop those; this is recommended for TypeScript, where type imports vanish at build time.

Cycles among test files are reported. Only migrations/ (and Python alembic/ and versions/) are excluded by default; add exclude = ["**/tests/**"] to silence test fixtures.

Each cycle finding lists every module of the strongly connected group in modules; edges is one representative closed loop (the shortest one through the alphabetically first module), so following it returns to its start.

docs.title: Boundaries
docs.text:
Each rule forbids any module matching from from importing any module matching to:

[[boundaries.forbidden]]
from = "app.domain"
to = "app.api"

Matching, per endpoint:

  • A plain name is a module-name prefix — app.domain matches app.domain and app.domain.*; for JavaScript and TypeScript modules, which are named by path, src/domain matches src/domain and src/domain/*.
  • A glob (* ? [) is matched against both the module name and the file path, so from = "**/domain/**" works even for namespace packages without __init__.py.
  • to also matches the literal import target, so rules still fire when an import cannot be resolved to an in-repo module.

A rule whose from matches no module is reported under meta.unmatched_boundary_rules in JSON output — a typo never looks like a clean pass.

docs.title: Accepting findings: [accept]
docs.text:
The out-of-line alternative to # noqa — nothing is written into your source. Keys are pillars or detector ids; values are substrings of the finding label as shown in a scan. The file is committed, so accepted findings stop flagging for every teammate and their agents:

[accept]
dead_code = ["legacy.compat::shim"]        # a specific accepted symbol
"smells/god_module" = ["app.registry"]     # a specific accepted detector hit
duplication = ["legacy-fork/"]             # an accepted copy location

duplication patterns work per location. A plain path substring drops the matching occurrences from every clone group, and a group stays reported while two or more other copies remain, so accepting a fork never hides duplication elsewhere. A pattern containing " + " matches the group label (a.ts + b.ts + c.ts) and hides that whole group.

There are three ways to silence findings — pick by scope:

Mechanism Scope Shared? Use for exclude globs Whole files/dirs, per pillar or global Yes (committed) Generated code, fixtures, migrations [accept] Specific findings Yes (committed) Accepted debt the team agrees on brainz_triage Specific findings No (local .sensez/) Personal review verdicts

docs.title: Global scope
docs.text:
roots = []                          # package roots; empty = auto-detect from project layout
exclude = ["**/generated/**"]       # excluded from every pillar

docs.title: Gate and local metrics
docs.text:
CLI scans are stateless and never persist parsed source facts. Long-lived MCP and LSP processes reuse analysis state in memory for their own lifetime:

[cache]
# Enables process-local reuse in MCP/LSP only; CLI scans always remain stateless.
enabled = false

[gate]
repeat_limit = 2   # how often the gate re-reports the same finding before auto-deferring

[self_improvement]
enabled = false    # stops even the on-disk recording under .sensez/local-metrics/

docs.title: Adopting Sensez in an existing repository
docs.text:
1. Run sensez noze . --summary for aggregated per-rule counts to see what would be noisy.
  2. Gate only on new work: run sensez noze . --diff --fail-on-new in CI (or use the GitHub Action), so the backlog does not block anyone.
  3. Record the agreed backlog in [accept] as you review it.
  4. Escalate action levels pillar by pillar as each one cleans up.

docs.title: Quieting a noisy detector
docs.text:
Prefer raising its threshold over disabling it, and scope the change to the language that is noisy:

[smells.python.rules.god_module]
min_fan = 40

Use enabled = false only as a last resort — a disabled detector is invisible in future scans.

docs.title: Fixing framework false positives
docs.text: Add the framework's registration pattern to [dead_code] (above) instead of suppressing findings one by one.

docs.title: Practical advice
docs.text:
• Keep the file small enough that a new contributor can scan it in one sitting.
  • Prefer explicit thresholds and exclusions over broad global disablement.
  • Treat the config as code: review changes to it the same way you would review a detector change.

docs.title: Boolean Blindness (boolean_blindness)
docs.text:
What it is

Bare booleans whose meaning is invisible at the call site (f(true, false)) — use a closed type (enum or literal union) or named options so calls read clearly.

Why it's bad

Call sites stop reading like code and start reading like truth tables.

Example

PythonJS / TS

Problem

def publish_invoice(
    invoice_id: str,
    email_customer: bool,
    archive_pdf: bool,
    notify_owner: bool,
) -> None:
    invoice = repo.load(invoice_id)
    if email_customer:
        mailer.send(invoice)
    else:
        review_queue.add(invoice)
    if archive_pdf:
        archive.store(render_pdf(invoice))
    if notify_owner:
        notifier.ping(invoice.owner)

Proposed fix

Promote each boolean decision into a named strategy so callers choose behavior explicitly.

from typing import Protocol


class InvoiceDelivery(Protocol):
    def deliver(self, invoice: Invoice) -> None: ...


class InvoiceFollowUp(Protocol):
    def run(self, invoice: Invoice) -> None: ...


class EmailDelivery:
    def deliver(self, invoice: Invoice) -> None:
        mailer.send(invoice)


class ReviewQueueDelivery:
    def deliver(self, invoice: Invoice) -> None:
        review_queue.add(invoice)


class PdfArchival:
    def run(self, invoice: Invoice) -> None:
        archive.store(render_pdf(invoice))


class OwnerNotification:
    def run(self, invoice: Invoice) -> None:
        notifier.ping(invoice.owner)


def publish_invoice(
    invoice_id: str,
    delivery: InvoiceDelivery,
    follow_ups: list[InvoiceFollowUp],
) -> None:
    invoice = repo.load(invoice_id)
    delivery.deliver(invoice)
    for follow_up in follow_ups:
        follow_up.run(invoice)

Problem

function publishInvoice(
  invoiceId: string,
  emailCustomer: boolean,
  archivePdf: boolean,
  notifyOwner: boolean,
): void {
  const invoice = repo.load(invoiceId);
  if (emailCustomer) {
    mailer.send(invoice);
  } else {
    reviewQueue.add(invoice);
  }
  if (archivePdf) {
    archive.store(renderPdf(invoice));
  }
  if (notifyOwner) {
    notifier.ping(invoice.owner);
  }
}

Proposed fix

Promote each boolean decision into a named strategy so callers choose behavior explicitly.

interface InvoiceDelivery {
  deliver(invoice: Invoice): void;
}

interface InvoiceFollowUp {
  run(invoice: Invoice): void;
}

class EmailDelivery implements InvoiceDelivery {
  deliver(invoice: Invoice): void {
    mailer.send(invoice);
  }
}

class ReviewQueueDelivery implements InvoiceDelivery {
  deliver(invoice: Invoice): void {
    reviewQueue.add(invoice);
  }
}

class PdfArchival implements InvoiceFollowUp {
  run(invoice: Invoice): void {
    archive.store(renderPdf(invoice));
  }
}

class OwnerNotification implements InvoiceFollowUp {
  run(invoice: Invoice): void {
    notifier.ping(invoice.owner);
  }
}

function publishInvoice(
  invoiceId: string,
  delivery: InvoiceDelivery,
  followUps: InvoiceFollowUp[],
): void {
  const invoice = repo.load(invoiceId);
  delivery.deliver(invoice);
  for (const followUp of followUps) {
    followUp.run(invoice);
  }
}

docs.title: Literal Membership (literal_membership)
docs.text:
What it is

Branching on membership in a literal string list, or on three or more ===/== string comparisons of one value joined by ||/or — stringly-typed categories; use a closed type (enum or literal union). Punctuation sets and markup tag names are outside vocabularies and stay quiet.

Why it's bad

Hard-coded string sets become a hidden enum that tools cannot help with.

Example

PythonJS / TS

Problem

def is_allowed(status: str) -> bool:
    return status in ["draft", "paid", "void"]

Proposed fix

Use an Enum or named constant set with a typed boundary.

from enum import Enum


class InvoiceStatus(Enum):
    DRAFT = "draft"
    PAID = "paid"
    VOID = "void"


def is_allowed(status: InvoiceStatus) -> bool:
    return status in {
        InvoiceStatus.DRAFT,
        InvoiceStatus.PAID,
        InvoiceStatus.VOID,
    }

Problem

function isAllowed(status: string): boolean {
  return ["draft", "paid", "void"].includes(status);
}

Proposed fix

Use a string-literal union type or a named as const set shared with its type.

enum InvoiceStatus {
  Draft = "draft",
  Paid = "paid",
  Void = "void",
}

function isAllowed(status: InvoiceStatus): boolean {
  return status === InvoiceStatus.Draft ||
    status === InvoiceStatus.Paid ||
    status === InvoiceStatus.Void;
}

docs.title: Magic String Default (magic_string_default)
docs.text:
What it is

A fallback empty, one-character, or placeholder string (?? "", or "n/a") is stored, compared, or returned in place of a missing value — the contract is hiding in a sentinel; prefer a nullable/optional string or a dedicated sum type.

Why it's bad

A sentinel string hides the real optionality of the value.

Example

PythonJS / TS LowMediumHigh

Flags empty, one-character, or sentinel-word fallbacks that are stored, sent, or compared.

Problem

def save_owner(owner: Owner) -> None:
    store.save(label=owner.label or "")

Proposed fix

Reject a missing required string explicitly instead of hiding it behind a sentinel fallback.

def display_name(name: str | None) -> str:
    if name is None:
        raise ValueError("display name is required")
    return name

Also flags empty or one-character fallbacks that are returned or kept in a variable; skips rendered text and string operations, including coercions such as Number(..) and lookups such as map.get(..).

Problem

def display_name(name: str | None) -> str:
    return name or ""

Proposed fix

Reject a missing required string explicitly instead of hiding it behind a sentinel fallback.

def display_name(name: str | None) -> str:
    if name is None:
        raise ValueError("display name is required")
    return name

Flags every empty, one-character, or sentinel-word fallback wherever it flows.

Problem

def greeting(name: str | None) -> str:
    return f"Hello {name or ''}"

Proposed fix

Reject a missing required string explicitly instead of hiding it behind a sentinel fallback.

def display_name(name: str | None) -> str:
    if name is None:
        raise ValueError("display name is required")
    return name
LowMediumHigh

Flags empty, one-character, or sentinel-word fallbacks that are stored, sent, or compared.

Problem

async function saveOwner(owner: Owner): Promise<void> {
  await store.save({ label: owner.label ?? "n/a" });
}

Proposed fix

Throw on a missing required string, or model optionality explicitly when absence is valid.

function displayName(name?: string): string {
  if (name === undefined) {
    throw new Error("display name is required");
  }
  return name;
}

Also flags empty or one-character fallbacks that are returned or kept in a variable; skips rendered text and string operations, including coercions such as Number(..) and lookups such as map.get(..).

Problem

function displayName(name?: string): string {
  return name || "?";
}

Proposed fix

Throw on a missing required string, or model optionality explicitly when absence is valid.

  if (name === undefined) {
    throw new Error("display name is required");
  }
  return name;
}

Flags every empty, one-character, or sentinel-word fallback wherever it flows.

Problem

function greeting(name?: string): string {
  return `Hello ${name ?? ""}`;
}

Proposed fix

docs.title: Magic Numbers (magic_numbers)
docs.text:
What it is

Unexplained numeric literals in logic — name them as constants so their intent is clear.

Why it's bad

Numbers without names are hard to audit and easy to copy blindly.

Example

PythonJS / TS

Problem

def is_retryable(attempts: int) -> bool:
    return attempts < 7

Proposed fix

Extract a named constant near the policy it represents.

MAX_RETRIES = 7


def is_retryable(attempts: int) -> bool:
    return attempts < MAX_RETRIES

Problem

function isRetryable(attempts: number): boolean {
  return attempts < 7;
}

Proposed fix

Use a named const or configuration value for the policy number.

const MAX_RETRIES = 7;

function isRetryable(attempts: number): boolean {
  return attempts < MAX_RETRIES;
}

docs.title: Deep Nesting (deep_nesting)
docs.text:
What it is

Control flow nests many levels deep, hard to follow — flatten with early returns or extracted helpers.

Why it's bad

The control flow becomes hard to scan and easy to misread in review.

Example

PythonJS / TS

Problem

def approve(order: Order) -> bool:
    if order.is_paid:
        if not order.is_flagged:
            if order.customer.is_active:
                if order.customer.is_verified:
                    if order.total < order.customer.limit:
                        return True
    return False

Proposed fix

Use guard clauses, continue early, or extract a helper for the nested branch.

def approve(order: Order) -> bool:
    if not order.is_paid or order.is_flagged:
        return False
    if not order.customer.is_active:
        return False
    if not order.customer.is_verified:
        return False
    return order.total < order.customer.limit

Problem

function approve(order: Order): boolean {
  if (order.isPaid) {
    if (!order.isFlagged) {
      if (order.customer.isActive) {
        if (order.customer.isVerified) {
          if (order.total < order.customer.limit) {
            return true;
          }
        }
      }
    }
  }
  return false;
}

Proposed fix

Flatten with early returns/continues or pull nested checks into named helpers.

function approve(order: Order): boolean {
  if (!order.isPaid || order.isFlagged) {
    return false;
  }
  if (!order.customer.isActive) {
    return false;
  }
  if (!order.customer.isVerified) {
    return false;
  }
  return order.total < order.customer.limit;
}

docs.title: High Cognitive Complexity (high_cognitive_complexity)
docs.text:
What it is

Hard for a human to follow — nested branches and loops weighted by depth; simplify or break it up.

Why it's bad

The reader has to simulate too many branches and nesting levels at once.

Example

PythonJS / TS

Problem

def score(order: Order) -> int:
    total = 0
    if order.paid:
        if order.customer.active:
            if not order.customer.suspended:
                if order.customer.verified:
                    if order.total >= 500:
                        total += 25
                    elif order.total >= 100:
                        total += 10
                    else:
                        total += 1
    return total

Proposed fix

Name the decision steps, flatten branches, and extract cohesive helpers.

NO_SCORE = 0
ENTERPRISE_ORDER_THRESHOLD = 500
LARGE_ORDER_THRESHOLD = 100
ENTERPRISE_ORDER_SCORE = 25
LARGE_ORDER_SCORE = 10
STANDARD_ORDER_SCORE = 1


def score(order: Order) -> int:
    if not can_score(order):
        return NO_SCORE
    return score_total(order.total)


def can_score(order: Order) -> bool:
    if not order.paid:
        return False
    if not order.customer.active:
        return False
    if order.customer.suspended:
        return False
    return order.customer.verified


def score_total(total: int) -> int:
    if total >= ENTERPRISE_ORDER_THRESHOLD:
        return ENTERPRISE_ORDER_SCORE
    if total >= LARGE_ORDER_THRESHOLD:
        return LARGE_ORDER_SCORE
    return STANDARD_ORDER_SCORE

Problem

function score(order: Order): number {
  let total = 0;
  if (order.paid) {
    if (order.customer.active) {
      if (!order.customer.suspended) {
        if (order.customer.verified) {
          if (order.total >= 500) {
            total += 25;
          } else if (order.total >= 100) {
            total += 10;
          } else {
            total += 1;
          }
        }
      }
    }
  }
  return total;
}

Proposed fix

Prefer guard clauses and small predicate functions over nested branches.

const NO_SCORE = 0;
const ENTERPRISE_ORDER_THRESHOLD = 500;
const LARGE_ORDER_THRESHOLD = 100;
const ENTERPRISE_ORDER_SCORE = 25;
const LARGE_ORDER_SCORE = 10;
const STANDARD_ORDER_SCORE = 1;

function score(order: Order): number {
  if (!canScore(order)) {
    return NO_SCORE;
  }
  return scoreTotal(order.total);
}

function canScore(order: Order): boolean {
  if (!order.paid) {
    return false;
  }
  if (!order.customer.active) {
    return false;
  }
  if (order.customer.suspended) {
    return false;
  }
  return order.customer.verified;
}

function scoreTotal(total: number): number {
  if (total >= ENTERPRISE_ORDER_THRESHOLD) {
    return ENTERPRISE_ORDER_SCORE;
  }
  if (total >= LARGE_ORDER_THRESHOLD) {
    return LARGE_ORDER_SCORE;
  }
  return STANDARD_ORDER_SCORE;
}

docs.title: High Cyclomatic Complexity (high_complexity)
docs.text:
What it is

Many independent paths through the function, so it's hard to test fully — decompose it.

Why it's bad

The function accumulates too many distinct paths to reason about confidently.

Example

PythonJS / TS

Problem

def choose_refund(order: Order) -> RefundDecision:
    if order.cancelled:
        return deny_refund(order, "cancelled")
    if order.fraud_review:
        return manual_review(order)
    if order.days_since_purchase > 30:
        return deny_refund(order, "expired")
    if order.damaged:
        return full_refund(order)
    if order.missing_items:
        return partial_refund(order)
    if order.vip_customer:
        return goodwill_credit(order)
    return deny_refund(order, "not_eligible")

Proposed fix

Use a dispatch table or split the branches into named operations.

from collections.abc import Callable


RefundHandler = Callable[[Order], RefundDecision]


REFUND_POLICY: dict[str, RefundHandler] = {
    "cancelled": deny_cancelled,
    "fraud_review": manual_review,
    "expired": deny_expired,
    "damaged": full_refund,
    "missing_items": partial_refund,
    "vip_customer": goodwill_credit,
}


def choose_refund(order: Order) -> RefundDecision:
    handler = REFUND_POLICY.get(order.refund_reason(), deny_not_eligible)
    return handler(order)

Problem

function chooseRefund(order: Order): RefundDecision {
  if (order.cancelled) {
    return denyRefund(order, "cancelled");
  }
  if (order.fraudReview) {
    return manualReview(order);
  }
  if (order.daysSincePurchase > 30) {
    return denyRefund(order, "expired");
  }
  if (order.damaged) {
    return fullRefund(order);
  }
  if (order.missingItems) {
    return partialRefund(order);
  }
  if (order.vipCustomer) {
    return goodwillCredit(order);
  }
  return denyRefund(order, "not_eligible");
}

Proposed fix

Use a map, strategy object, or smaller functions for independent paths.

type RefundHandler = (order: Order) => RefundDecision;

const refundPolicy: Record<string, RefundHandler> = {
  cancelled: denyCancelled,
  fraud_review: manualReview,
  expired: denyExpired,
  damaged: fullRefund,
  missing_items: partialRefund,
  vip_customer: goodwillCredit,
};

function chooseRefund(order: Order): RefundDecision {
  const handler = refundPolicy[order.refundReason()] ?? denyNotEligible;
  return handler(order);
}

docs.title: Too Many Returns (too_many_returns)
docs.text:
What it is

Many exit points make the function's flow hard to follow — consolidate, or it's doing too much.

Why it's bad

Many exit points make the function harder to follow and test.

Example

PythonJS / TS

Problem

def status_for(order: Order) -> str:
    if order.cancelled:
        return "cancelled"
    elif order.refunded:
        return "refunded"
    elif order.failed:
        return "failed"
    elif order.paid:
        return "paid"
    return "open"

Proposed fix

Group related guards or extract decision helpers.

def status_for(order: Order) -> str:
    rules = (
        (order.cancelled, "cancelled"),
        (order.refunded, "refunded"),
        (order.failed, "failed"),
        (order.paid, "paid"),
    )
    for applies, status in rules:
        if applies:
            return status
    return "open"

Problem

function statusFor(order: Order): string {
  if (order.cancelled) {
    return "cancelled";
  } else if (order.refunded) {
    return "refunded";
  } else if (order.failed) {
    return "failed";
  } else if (order.paid) {
    return "paid";
  }
  return "open";
}

Proposed fix

Keep meaningful guard clauses, then extract noisy branches into predicates.

const ORDER_STATUS_RULES: Array<[keyof Order, string]> = [
  ["cancelled", "cancelled"],
  ["refunded", "refunded"],
  ["failed", "failed"],
  ["paid", "paid"],
];

function statusFor(order: Order): string {
  for (const [field, status] of ORDER_STATUS_RULES) {
    if (order[field]) {
      return status;
    }
  }
  return "open";
}

docs.title: Nested Ternary (nested_ternary)
docs.text:
What it is

A conditional expression is a branch or condition of another conditional expression, forcing readers to match several branches mentally — extract the result into a named function or flatten it into if statements with early returns.

Why it's bad

Nested conditional expressions force readers to mentally match several conditions with their results, making agent-generated logic difficult to review and change.

Example

PythonJS / TS MediumHigh

Flags direct chains, where one conditional is a branch or condition of another.

Problem

def delivery_status(order: Order) -> DeliveryStatus:
    return (
        DeliveryStatus.READY
        if order.is_paid
        else DeliveryStatus.RETRY
        if order.payment_retry_allowed
        else DeliveryStatus.BLOCKED
    )

Proposed fix

Extract the decision into a named helper, or replace the expression with ordered if statements and early returns.

def delivery_status(order) -> DeliveryStatus:
    if order.is_paid:
        return DeliveryStatus.READY
    if order.payment_retry_allowed:
        return DeliveryStatus.RETRY
    return DeliveryStatus.BLOCKED

Also flags conditionals nested inside a call argument or template of another; JSX elements and object literals end the nesting.

Problem

def delivery_label(order: Order) -> str:
    return (
        format_label("gift" if order.is_gift else "standard")
        if order.is_paid
        else "pending"
    )

Proposed fix

Extract the decision into a named helper, or replace the expression with ordered if statements and early returns.

def delivery_status(order) -> DeliveryStatus:
    if order.is_paid:
        return DeliveryStatus.READY
    if order.payment_retry_allowed:
        return DeliveryStatus.RETRY
    return DeliveryStatus.BLOCKED
MediumHigh

Flags direct chains, where one conditional is a branch or condition of another.

Problem

export function deliveryStatus(order: Order): DeliveryStatus {
  return order.isPaid
    ? DeliveryStatus.Ready
    : order.paymentRetryAllowed
      ? DeliveryStatus.Retry
      : DeliveryStatus.Blocked;
}

Proposed fix

Move result selection into a named function and use explicit if branches with early returns.

function deliveryStatus(order: Order): DeliveryStatus {
  if (order.isPaid) {
    return DeliveryStatus.Ready;
  }
  if (order.paymentRetryAllowed) {
    return DeliveryStatus.Retry;
  }
  return DeliveryStatus.Blocked;
}

Also flags conditionals nested inside a call argument or template of another; JSX elements and object literals end the nesting.

Problem

export function deliveryLabel(order: Order): string {
  return order.isPaid ? formatLabel(order.isGift ? "gift" : "standard") : "pending";
}

Proposed fix

Move result selection into a named function and use explicit if branches with early returns.

function deliveryStatus(order: Order): DeliveryStatus {
  if (order.isPaid) {
    return DeliveryStatus.Ready;
  }
  if (order.paymentRetryAllowed) {
    return DeliveryStatus.Retry;
  }
  return DeliveryStatus.Blocked;
}

docs.title: Unnecessary Nested If (unnecessary_nested_if)
docs.text:
What it is

An if whose only body is another if, with no else path — combine the conditions with and/&& to flatten the control flow.

Why it's bad

The code says 'if' twice when the condition really belongs on one line.

Example

Problem

    if order.paid:
        if order.address.is_valid:
            return True
    return False

Combine the conditions or use a guard clause.

def can_ship(order: Order) -> bool:
    if not order.paid:
        return False
    return order.address.is_valid

function canShip(order: Order): boolean {
  if (order.paid) {
    if (order.address.isValid) {
      return true;
    }
  }
  return false;
}

Proposed fix

Collapse nested conditions with && or extract a predicate.

  if (!order.paid) {

  return order.address.isValid;
}

docs.title: Redundant Validation (redundant_validation)
docs.text:
What it is

The same condition is checked repeatedly in one function — establish the invariant once and simplify the later path.

Why it's bad

Example

    if message is None:
        return
    prepare(message)
    if message is None:
        return
    send(message)

Proposed fix

def publish(message):
    if message is None:
        return
    prepare(message)
    send(message)

function publish(message: Message | undefined) {
  if (message === undefined) return;
  prepare(message);
  if (message === undefined) return;
  send(message);
}

Proposed fix

Validate at the boundary or first use, then rely on the established invariant.

  if (message === undefined) return;
  prepare(message);

docs.title: God Module (god_module)
docs.text:
What it is

A sizeable module with its own functions or classes that many modules depend on and that itself depends on many internal modules at runtime (high centrality) — a coupling and change-risk hotspot; split its responsibilities. A composition root of imports and one data object is not one.

Why it's bad

A single module becomes a hot spot with too many reasons to change.

Example

The example is kept short, so it fires with these settings:

# The example stays small; at defaults a god module needs a fan of 25, 150 lines
# and 12 functions or classes, and with four callers shotgun_surgery_hazard wins.
[smells]
god_module_fan = 4
god_module_min_fan_in = 4
god_module_min_fan_out = 4
god_module_min_lines = 0
god_module_min_units = 0
shotgun_blast_threshold = 5
PythonJS / TS

Problem

from god_module.dep_a import run as load_user
from god_module.dep_b import run as charge_user
from god_module.dep_c import run as send_receipt
from god_module.dep_d import run as archive_receipt


def process_checkout() -> int:
    return load_user() + charge_user() + send_receipt() + archive_receipt()

Proposed fix

Split by dependency direction and cohesive responsibility.

def load_user(user_id: str) -> User:
    return users.find(user_id)


def charge_user(user: User) -> Receipt:
    return billing.charge(user)


def send_receipt(user: User, receipt: Receipt) -> None:
    mailer.send(user.email, receipt)


def archive_receipt(receipt: Receipt) -> None:
    archive.save(receipt)

Problem

import { run as loadUser } from "./dep_a";
import { run as chargeUser } from "./dep_b";
import { run as sendReceipt } from "./dep_c";
import { run as archiveReceipt } from "./dep_d";

export function processCheckout(): number {
  return loadUser() + chargeUser() + sendReceipt() + archiveReceipt();
}

Proposed fix

Extract smaller modules and route callers through a narrow public API.

function loadUser(userId: string): User {
  return users.find(userId);
}

function chargeUser(user: User): Receipt {
  return billing.charge(user);
}

function sendReceipt(user: User, receipt: Receipt): void {
  mailer.send(user.email, receipt);
}

function archiveReceipt(receipt: Receipt): void {
  archive.save(receipt);
}

docs.title: Heavy Nested Function (heavy_nested_function)
docs.text:
What it is

An inner/nested function that grew large and logic-heavy — promote it to a top-level, testable function.

Why it's bad

Nested helpers hide important behavior and make tests awkward.

Example

The example is kept short, so it fires with these settings:

# The example stays short; at defaults the nested function needs more than 15 lines.
[smells]
max_nested_function_lines = 4
PythonJS / TS

Problem

def import_customers(rows: list[dict[str, str]]) -> list[Customer]:
    def normalize(row: dict[str, str]) -> Customer:
        email = row["email"].strip().lower()
        status = row["status"].strip()
        plan = row["plan"].strip()
        region = row["region"].strip()
        return Customer(email, status, plan, region)

    return [normalize(row) for row in rows]

Proposed fix

Promote the helper to a top-level private function with direct tests.

def normalize_customer(row: Row) -> Customer:
    email = row["email"].strip().lower()
    status = row["status"].strip()
    plan = row["plan"].strip()
    region = row["region"].strip()
    return Customer(email, status, plan, region)


def import_customers(rows: Rows) -> Customers:
    return [normalize_customer(row) for row in rows]

Problem

function importCustomers(rows: Row[]): Customer[] {
  function normalize(row: Row): Customer {
    const email = row.email.trim().toLowerCase();
    const status = row.status.trim();
    const plan = row.plan.trim();
    const region = row.region.trim();
    return new Customer(email, status, plan, region);
  }

  return rows.map(normalize);
}

Proposed fix

Move the nested function to module scope or a small collaborator.

function normalizeCustomer(row: Row): Customer {
  const email = row.email.trim().toLowerCase();
  const status = row.status.trim();
  const plan = row.plan.trim();
  const region = row.region.trim();
  return new Customer(email, status, plan, region);
}

function importCustomers(rows: Row[]): Customer[] {
  return rows.map(normalizeCustomer);
}

What it is

docs.title: Long Function (long_function)
docs.text:
What it is

Too many lines to grasp at once — extract cohesive pieces. Related code-smell reference: Refactoring.Guru: Long Method.

Why it's bad

The function becomes a scroll instead of a unit you can hold in your head.

Example

PythonJS / TS

Problem

def import_orders(rows: Rows) -> Orders:
    parsed = [parse_order(row) for row in rows]
    valid = [order for order in parsed if order.is_valid]
    enriched = [enrich(order) for order in valid]
    totals = [calculate_total(order) for order in enriched]
    discounts = [calculate_discount(order) for order in enriched]
    taxes = [calculate_tax(order) for order in enriched]
    save_orders(enriched)
    notify_import_complete(enriched)
    archive_totals(totals)
    archive_discounts(discounts)
    archive_taxes(taxes)
    return enriched

Proposed fix

Extract named chunks that each complete one step of the workflow.

def import_orders(rows: Rows) -> Orders:
    orders = _valid_orders(rows)
    enriched = [enrich(order) for order in orders]
    _persist_import(enriched)
    return enriched


def _valid_orders(rows: Rows) -> Orders:
    parsed = [parse_order(row) for row in rows]
    return [order for order in parsed if order.is_valid]


def _persist_import(orders: Orders) -> None:
    save_orders(orders)
    notify_import_complete(orders)
    archive_totals([calculate_total(order) for order in orders])

Problem

function importOrders(rows: Rows): Orders {
  const parsed = rows.map(parseOrder);
  const valid = parsed.filter((order) => order.isValid);
  const enriched = valid.map(enrich);
  const totals = enriched.map(calculateTotal);
  const discounts = enriched.map(calculateDiscount);
  const taxes = enriched.map(calculateTax);
  saveOrders(enriched);
  notifyImportComplete(enriched);
  archiveTotals(totals);
  archiveDiscounts(discounts);
  archiveTaxes(taxes);
  return enriched;
}

Proposed fix

Extract cohesive helper functions and keep the orchestration readable.

function importOrders(rows: Rows): Orders {
  const orders = validOrders(rows);
  const enriched = orders.map(enrich);
  persistImport(enriched);
  return enriched;
}

function validOrders(rows: Rows): Orders {
  const parsed = rows.map(parseOrder);
  return parsed.filter((order) => order.isValid);
}

function persistImport(orders: Orders): void {
  saveOrders(orders);
  notifyImportComplete(orders);
  archiveTotals(orders.map(calculateTotal));
}

docs.title: Narrating Code (narrating_code)
docs.text:
What it is

A function is packed with step-by-step narration or commented-out code — prefer clearer names or extracted helpers, delete dead code, and keep comments for why.

Why it's bad

The prose becomes a second implementation that readers must keep in sync with the code.

Example

PythonJS / TS

Problem

def activate_plan(account: Account) -> None:
    # Load the account owner.
    owner = account.owner
    # Load the billing profile.
    billing = owner.billing_profile
    # Check whether billing is enabled.
    if not billing.enabled:
        return
    # Load the selected plan.
    plan = billing.selected_plan
    # Activate the selected plan.
    account.activate(plan)
    # Notify the owner.
    notify_owner(owner, plan)

Proposed fix

Rename values and extract helper functions so the code says what the comments were saying.

def activate_plan(account: Account) -> None:
    owner = account.owner
    billing = owner.billing_profile
    if not billing.enabled:
        return
    _activate_selected_plan(account, owner, billing)


def _activate_selected_plan(
    account: Account,
    owner: Owner,
    billing: BillingProfile,
) -> None:
    plan = billing.selected_plan
    account.activate(plan)
    notify_owner(owner, plan)

function activatePlan(account: Account): void {
  // Load the account owner.
  const owner = account.owner;
  // Load the billing profile.
  const billing = owner.billingProfile;
  // Check whether billing is enabled.

    return;
  }
  // Load the selected plan.
  const plan = billing.selectedPlan;
  // Activate the selected plan.
  account.activate(plan);
  // Notify the owner.
  notifyOwner(owner, plan);
}

Proposed fix

Extract named predicates/helpers and keep comments for constraints or rationale.

  const owner = account.owner;
  const billing = owner.billingProfile;
  if (!billing.enabled) {
    return;
  }
  activateSelectedPlan(account, owner, billing);
}

  account: Account,
  owner: Owner,
  billing: BillingProfile,

docs.title: Data Clump (data_clump)
docs.text:
What it is

The same group of values is passed together through many functions — bundle them into one object or typed structure. Related code-smell reference: Refactoring.Guru: Data Clumps.

Why it's bad

The same bundle has to be kept in sync everywhere it travels.

Example

PythonJS / TS

Problem

def format_label(street: str, city: str, zip_code: str, country: str) -> str:
    return f"{street}, {city} {zip_code}, {country}"


def shipping_zone(street: str, city: str, zip_code: str, country: str) -> str:
    return zones.lookup(street, city, zip_code, country)

    return carriers.covers(street, city, zip_code, country)

    city: str
    zip_code: str
    country: str


def format_label(address: Address) -> str:

    return zones.lookup(address)

docs.title: Divergent Change (divergent_change)
docs.text:
What it is

One module gets edited for many unrelated reasons — it has too many responsibilities; split it along those axes. Related code-smell reference: Refactoring.Guru: Divergent Change.

Why it's bad

One file starts changing for unrelated reasons, so fixes get tangled.

Example

PythonJS / TS

Problem

class InvoiceReport:
    def render_header(self) -> str:
        return self.title.upper()

    def calculate_total(self) -> float:
        return self.subtotal + self.tax

    def save_archive(self) -> None:
        archive.write(self.path)

Proposed fix

Split the module by reason-to-change: presentation, pricing, persistence, etc.

class InvoiceRenderer:
    def render_header(self, invoice: Invoice) -> str:
        return invoice.title.upper()


class InvoiceTotals:
    def calculate_total(self, invoice: Invoice) -> float:
        return invoice.subtotal + invoice.tax


class InvoiceArchive:
    def save(self, invoice: Invoice) -> None:
        archive.write(invoice.path)

Problem

docs.text:
What it is

An abstraction has only two implementations that grow in different directions — remove the forced common type or narrow it to genuine shared behavior.

docs.title: Feature Envy (feature_envy)
docs.text:
What it is

A method uses another object's data more than its own — move it onto the class that owns that data. Related code-smell reference: Refactoring.Guru: Feature Envy.

Why it's bad

Logic sits next to the wrong data, so edits keep reaching through a foreign object.

Example

PythonJS / TS

Problem

class Account:
    balance: int
    fee_rate: int
    limit: int


class BillingPolicy:
    name: str

    def fee_for(self, account: Account) -> tuple[str, int]:
        fee = account.balance + account.fee_rate + account.limit
        return self.name, fee

Proposed fix

Move the behavior onto the object that owns most of the data.

class Account:
    balance: int
    fee_rate: int
    limit: int

    def billing_fee(self) -> int:
        return self.balance + self.fee_rate + self.limit


class BillingPolicy:
    name: str

    def fee_for(self, account: Account) -> tuple[str, int]:
        return self.name, account.billing_fee()

class Account {
  balance = 0;
  feeRate = 0;
  limit = 0;
}

  name = "standard";

  feeFor(account: Account): [string, number] {
    const fee = account.balance + account.feeRate + account.limit;
    return [this.name, fee];
  }
}

Proposed fix

Put the calculation on the owning class/module or expose a narrow query method.

class Account {
  balance = 0;
  feeRate = 0;
  limit = 0;

  billingFee(): number {
    return this.balance + this.feeRate + this.limit;
  }
}

  name = "standard";

  feeFor(account: Account): [string, number] {
    return [this.name, account.billingFee()];

docs.title: Inappropriate Intimacy (inappropriate_intimacy)
docs.text:
What it is

Two classes each reach into the other's internals, so neither can change independently — narrow the shared surface or merge them. Related code-smell reference: Refactoring.Guru: Inappropriate Intimacy.

Why it's bad

Two classes know too much about each other's internals, so refactors ripple.

Example

PythonJS / TS

Problem

class Account:
    def __init__(self) -> None:
        self._token = "secret"
        self._salt = "pepper"


def audit_account() -> str:
    account: Account = Account()
    return account._token + account._salt

Proposed fix

Add a public method on the collaborator or merge the coupled objects.

    def __init__(self) -> None:
        self._token = "secret"
        self._salt = "pepper"

    def audit_key(self) -> str:
        return self._token + self._salt


def audit_account() -> str:
    account = Account()
    return account.audit_key()

  _token = "secret";
  _salt = "pepper";
}

  const account: Account = new Account();
  return account._token + account._salt;

  private token = "secret";
  private salt = "pepper";

  auditKey(): string {

docs.title: Message Chain (message_chain)
docs.text:
What it is

A long a.b.c.d access chain couples the caller to a deep object graph (Law of Demeter) — ask the immediate collaborator instead. Related code-smell reference: Refactoring.Guru: Message Chains.

Deep property walking couples the caller to the whole object graph.

Example

Problem

    return order.customer.address.city.country.name

Ask the nearest object for the answer through a method or property.

    def shipping_country(self) -> str:
        return self.customer.shipping_country()

    def shipping_country(self) -> str:
        return self.address.country_name()


class Address:
    def country_name(self) -> str:
        return self.city.country_name()


class City:
    def country_name(self) -> str:
        return self.country.name


def country(order: Order) -> str:

  return order.customer.address.city.country.name;
}

docs.title: Refused Bequest (refused_bequest)
docs.text:
What it is

A subclass inherits methods/fields it doesn't use or stubs out — the inheritance is wrong; prefer composition. Related code-smell reference: Refactoring.Guru: Refused Bequest.

Inheritance promises behavior the subclass does not actually want.

Example

Problem

class Report:
    def export_pdf(self) -> bytes:
        return render_pdf(self)

    def send_email(self) -> None:
        mailer.send(self)

    def export_pdf(self) -> bytes:

    def send_email(self) -> None:
        raise NotImplementedError

    def export_pdf(self) -> bytes:

    throw new Error("not supported");
  }
}

docs.title: Shotgun Surgery Hazard (shotgun_surgery_hazard)
docs.text:
What it is

A symbol so widely depended-on that one change ripples across many modules — a blast-radius hotspot. Related code-smell reference: Refactoring.Guru: Shotgun Surgery.

One edit fans out to many dependents.

Problem

def calculate(amount: float) -> float:
    return amount * TAX_RATE

Separate stable interfaces from volatile implementation details.

    def __init__(self, rate: float) -> None:

}

  constructor(private readonly rate: number) {}

  calculate(amount: number): number {
    return amount * this.rate;

What it is

docs.title: Implicit Schema (implicit_schema)

What it is

A dict/object accessed by many string keys — an unwritten schema; model it as a typed structure.

Why it's bad

interface UserPayload {
  email: string;
  plan: string;
  active: boolean;
  seats: number;

docs.text:
What it is

A function body silences the type checker (as any, as unknown as T, a bare @ts-ignore or # type: ignore, cast(Any, …)) instead of giving the value a type — the types and the code disagree and nobody looked. Body casts belong to this rule; signatures belong to loose_typing.

docs.title: Tuple Packing (tuple_packing)
docs.text:
What it is

Data passed as positional tuples whose fields aren't named — use a named structure so meaning is explicit.

Why it's bad

Positional bundles hide meaning and make the code brittle to reorderings.

docs.title: Defensive Fallback Soup (defensive_fallback)
docs.text:
What it is

Broad error handling and repeated empty defaults hide invalid states — validate the boundary and let unexpected failures remain visible.

Why it's bad

        options = raw.get("options") or {}
        return names, options
    except:
        return [], {}

Proposed fix

def load_payload(raw):

        return Payload.parse(raw)
    except InvalidPayload as error:

docs.title: Swallowed Error Sentinel (swallowed_error_sentinel)
docs.text:
What it is

An error handler drops the error and returns a placeholder (null, [], false) or only logs — callers get a plausible value instead of a failure; rethrow or return a typed failure.

Why it's bad

A handler that turns any failure into null, an empty list or a log line hands callers a plausible value; the broken contract surfaces far from its cause, or never.

Example

PythonJS / TS LowMedium

Flags handlers that return an empty value (null, None, [], false), except around a single JSON parse.

Problem

def load_profile(profile_id):
    try:
        return client.profiles.get(profile_id)
    except Exception as error:
        log.warning("profile load failed: %s", error)
        return None

Proposed fix

Catch the specific exception you can handle, re-raise the rest with raise ... from error, or return a typed failure the caller must check.

def load_profile(profile_id):
    try:
        return client.profiles.get(profile_id)
    except ClientError as error:
        raise ProfileUnavailable(profile_id) from error

Also flags empty-value returns around a single JSON parse.

docs.text:
What it is

The function mutates a caller's argument in place — a hidden side effect; return a new value instead.

docs.title: Name Promise Mismatch (name_promise_mismatch)
docs.text:
What it is

A function named like a read (get, is, find, validate, ...) also writes state — rename it to say so or move the write to the caller.

Why it's bad

Callers trust a read-named function to be safe to call twice, cache, or skip; a hidden write breaks all three.

Example

PythonJS / TS LowMediumHigh

Flags only database, network and scheduling writes.

Problem

def get_invoice(db: Database, invoice_id: str) -> Invoice | None:
    invoice = db.invoices.find(invoice_id)
    if invoice is None:
        db.invoices.insert({"id": invoice_id, "status": "draft"})
    return invoice

Proposed fix

Rename it to name the write (get_or_create_invoice), or return the data and let the caller write.

    invoice = db.invoices.find(invoice_id)
    if invoice is not None:
        return invoice
    return db.invoices.insert({"id": invoice_id, "status": "draft"})

Also flags mutating calls and assignments on parameters, own members and module-level names; skips caches and lazy initialisation.

docs.title: Split Variable (split_variable)
docs.text:
What it is

One local is reassigned to mean different things at different points — use distinct, single-purpose bindings.

Why it's bad

A variable with multiple meanings is a trap for both readers and debuggers.

Example

PythonJS / TS

Problem

def invoice_total(invoice: Invoice) -> float:
    result = sum(item.price for item in invoice.items)
    result = result - invoice.discount
    result = result + invoice.tax
    return result

Use separate locals named for each meaning.

def invoice_total(invoice: Invoice) -> float:
    subtotal = sum(item.price for item in invoice.items)
    discounted_total = subtotal - invoice.discount
    return discounted_total + invoice.tax

  let result = sum(invoice.items.map((item) => item.price));
  result = result - invoice.discount;
  result = result + invoice.tax;
  result = roundCurrency(result);
  return result;
}

Proposed fix

Prefer distinct const bindings for distinct concepts.

function invoiceTotal(invoice: Invoice): number {
  const subtotal = sum(invoice.items.map((item) => item.price));
  const discountedTotal = subtotal - invoice.discount;
  return discountedTotal + invoice.tax;
}

docs.title: Nested Loop (nested_loop)
docs.text:
What it is

A loop is nested directly or through a helper called inside a loop — work grows multiplicatively; combine passes or pre-index the data.

Why it's bad

Costs grow faster than the data and the code gets hard to flatten.

Example

PythonJS / TS

Problem

def find_matches(users: list[User], orders: list[Order]) -> list[tuple[User, Order]]:
    matches = []
    for user in users:
        for order in orders:
            if order.user_id == user.id:
                matches.append((user, order))
    return matches

Proposed fix

Pre-index one side, combine passes, or use a clearer iterator pipeline.

def find_matches(users: list[User], orders: list[Order]) -> list[tuple[User, Order]]:
    orders_by_user = {order.user_id: order for order in orders}
    matches = []
    for user in users:
        order = orders_by_user.get(user.id)
        if order is not None:
            matches.append((user, order))
    return matches

Problem

function findMatches(users: User[], orders: Order[]): Array<[User, Order]> {
  const matches: Array<[User, Order]> = [];
  for (const user of users) {
    for (const order of orders) {
      if (order.userId === user.id) {
        matches.push([user, order]);
      }
    }
  }
  return matches;
}

Proposed fix

Build a lookup map or flatten the data before iterating.

function findMatches(users: User[], orders: Order[]): Array<[User, Order]> {
  const ordersByUser = indexOrdersByUser(orders);
  const matches: Array<[User, Order]> = [];
  for (const user of users) {
    const order = ordersByUser.get(user.id);
    if (order) {
      matches.push([user, order]);
    }
  }
  return matches;
}

function indexOrdersByUser(orders: Order[]): Map<string, Order> {
  const ordersByUser = new Map<string, Order>();
  for (const order of orders) {
    ordersByUser.set(order.userId, order);
  }
  return ordersByUser;
}

docs.title: N+1 Loop Call (n_plus_one_call)
docs.text:
What it is

An external-looking call runs once per loop item — prefer a bulk query/request or prefetch so work scales by batch, not item.

Why it's bad

A per-item call can explode runtime and hit the backend one request at a time.

Example

PythonJS / TS

Problem

def load_profiles(api: ProfileApi, users: list[User]) -> list[Profile]:
    profiles = []
    for user in users:
        profiles.append(api.fetch(user.id))
    return profiles

Proposed fix

Batch-load or prefetch the related data before the loop.

def load_profiles(api: ProfileApi, users: list[User]) -> list[Profile]:
    ids = [user.id for user in users]
    profiles = api.fetch_many(ids)
    return [profiles[user_id] for user_id in ids]

Problem

function loadProfiles(api: ProfileApi, users: User[]): Profile[] {
  const profiles = [];
  for (const user of users) {
    profiles.push(api.fetch(user.id));
  }
  return profiles;
}

Proposed fix

Use a bulk endpoint/query or prefetch into a map before rendering.

async function loadProfiles(api: ProfileApi, users: User[]): Promise<Profile[]> {
  const ids = users.map((user) => user.id);
  const profiles = await api.fetchMany(ids);
  return ids.map((id) => profiles[id]);
}

docs.title: Repeated Iteration (repeated_iteration)
docs.text:
What it is

The same collection gets three or more passes, two loops, or two passes where one folds it (reduce, sum, filter(..).length), in one scope with nothing forcing them apart — fuse the passes so the data is scanned once. Field projections, rendered lists and Set/Map indexes built from a pass do not count.

Why it's bad

The same collection gets scanned over and over when one pass would do.

Example

PythonJS / TS

Problem

def summarize(items: Items) -> Summary:
    has_items = any(items)
    total = sum(items)
    return Summary(has_items=has_items, total=total)

Proposed fix

Fuse compatible passes or cache the intermediate result.

def summarize(items: Items) -> Summary:
    has_items = False
    total = 0
    for item in items:
        has_items = True
        total += item
    return Summary(has_items=has_items, total=total)

Problem

function summarize(items: Items): Summary {
  const paid = items.filter((item) => item.paid).length;
  const total = items.reduce((sum, item) => sum + item.price, 0);
  return { paid, total };
}

Proposed fix

Combine loops when the operations share the same traversal.

function summarize(items: Items): Summary {
  let paid = 0;
  let total = 0;
  for (const item of items) {
    if (item.paid) {
      paid += 1;
    }
    total += item.price;
  }
  return { paid, total };
}

docs.title: Sort In Loop (sort_in_loop)

What it is

A collection is sorted inside a loop — hoist sorting or maintain ordered data to avoid repeated O(n log n) work.

Why it's bad

Repeated sorts turn a small loop into a surprisingly expensive one.

}

  const names: string[] = [];
  for (const group of groups) {

  return names;
}

docs.title: Fixture Echo Assertion (fixture_echo_assertion)

What it is
